stem:
A 64-year-old with a previous myocardial infarction has a regular broad-complex tachycardia at 190/min with a palpable carotid pulse, blood pressure 72/44 mmHg and drowsiness. Under sedation from a senior emergency physician, three synchronised shocks have been delivered. Each produced a few sinus beats before the same tachycardia returned; he still has a pulse and remains hypotensive. Potassium and magnesium are being checked.

What is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.text: Switch to unsynchronised shocks at maximum energy
options.explanation: He has a pulse and an organised rhythm; an unsynchronised shock risks landing on the T wave and causing VF.

options.label: B
options.text: Amiodarone, then a further synchronised shock
options.explanation: When synchronised cardioversion fails in unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, guidelines add an amiodarone loading dose over 10–20 minutes and repeat the synchronised shock, while correcting electrolytes.

options.label: C
options.text: Give intravenous adenosine as a rapid bolus
options.explanation: Adenosine is for regular narrow-complex tachycardia and will not terminate VT after a myocardial infarction.

options.label: D
options.text: Give intravenous verapamil by slow injection
options.explanation: Verapamil can cause profound hypotension and collapse in ventricular tachycardia, particularly when already hypotensive.

options.label: E
options.text: Start CPR and give adrenaline 1 mg intravenously
options.explanation: He has a palpable pulse, so cardiac arrest treatment is not indicated.

context: In unstable ventricular tachycardia with a pulse, use synchronised cardioversion; if three shocks fail, give amiodarone and repeat the synchronised shock rather than switching to unsynchronised shocks.
